entry.title: From enforcement to trust
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / From enforcement to trustFrom enforcement to trust

After process reforms, GST needs road map to shed exclusions

premium

The broader unfinished agenda for GST’s full benefits to accrue to the economy is the inclusion of items such as petrol, diesel, electricity and natural gas that remain outside its ambit

Business Standard Editorial Comment4 min read Last Updated : Oct 11 2026 | 10:44 PM ISTWhen India rolled out goods and services tax (GST) on July 1, 2017, there was a concern that the bureaucracy grappled with — the uncertainty about the revenue trajectory and the need to compensate the states for any revenue shortfall in the first five years of the new tax. One source of revenue was proceeds of the GST compensation cess levied on items such as automobiles and tobacco. The other way to address the revenue risk was to have enough checks to prevent evasion. The tax system, thus, remained geared to ensure compliance, but at the expense of procedural simplicity. But officials’ worry about revenue collection and unmanageable compensation requirement did turn out to be true when the first Covid-19 wave hit India, and GST revenues plummeted in April 2020.  Monthly gross GST receipts of the central and state governments, which averaged ₹95,515 crore in 2018-19 and ₹96,605 crore in 2019-20, fell to ₹32,172 crore in April 2020. Consequently, the central government had to borrow ₹2.69 trillion from the market to compensate the states for their revenue shortfall. The full repayment of that in 2025-26 offered the GST Council an opportunity in September last year to review the tax slabs and rates, phase out the cess, and offer a consumption stimulus by lowering the indirect tax on a range of daily use as well as aspirational items, ranging from toothpaste and shampoo to consumer electronics and cars in the biggest overhaul of the system. Also, the number of slabs was brought down to broadly two, 5 and 18 per cent, from the earlier four—5, 12, 18 and 28 per cent with cess. That helped to boost consumption demand. Private final consumption expenditure expanded 7.1 per cent in the March quarter of 2025-26 as compared to 5.6 per cent at the same time a year earlier.  The next logical step for reform obviously was cutting red tape and making life simpler for businesses. The tech-enabled tax system, which captures a large amount of data from multiple sources, has made it possible for the authorities to spot sources of revenue leakage. The GST Council’s decisions last week — to drop the arrest provision, lower the penalty from ₹25,000 to ₹10,000, recall notices issued for amounts below ₹10,000 and not to issue such notices in future, offer credits for taxes paid on input services from November and on capital goods from April next year, and simplify the norms for GST registration and refunds — are a major structural overhaul of the tax system. The prosecution threshold is also being raised from ₹1 crore to  ₹5 crore. These measures mark the transformation from a framework designed to deal with tax evasion by a few to one that facilitates honest tax payers based on trust.  However, the task is not over. Two proposals, one meant to offer annual return filing and quarterly tax payments to consumer-facing businesses with sales up to ₹5 crore and a second proposal to further ease input tax credit availability, are sought to be implemented from April next year after another round of deliberation. The broader unfinished agenda for GST’s full benefits to accrue to the economy is the inclusion of items such as petrol, diesel, electricity and natural gas that remain outside its ambit. If the tax rates are indeed going to be reviewed only once a year from hereon, that should free up the Council’s bandwidth to discuss and lay out a road map for such excluded items so that efficiencies and competitiveness are enhanced across the value chain and GST truly becomes “good and simple”.   Topics : GST goods and service tax GST Council cgst GST Act BS Opinion Business Standard Editorial Comment

entry.title: Reality check at Nagoya
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / Reality check at NagoyaReality check at Nagoya

India needs a more focused approach in sports

premium

With 85 medals, India came in fourth, thanks to a flurry of medals in the last few days

Business Standard Editorial Comment3 min read Last Updated : Oct 06 2026 | 7:03 PM ISTIndia’s performance at the recently concluded Asian Games at Nagoya, Japan, was worryingly underwhelming, both by its own standards and when measured against its Asian peers. With 85 medals, India came in fourth, thanks to a flurry of medals in the last few days. The Indian women’s hockey team offered a triumph by beating China to win gold after 44 years, handing India a rare double with the men winning gold by prevailing over Malaysia. Teenager Kumkum Mohod’s individual recurve gold — making her the first Indian to do so— added to the lustre. But Nagoya’s total medal haul was considerably lower than the 107 India won in the previous edition of the Asian Games in Hangzhou, China.  In sports where India has a strong advantage such as badminton, India failed to win an individual medal for the first time in 12 years. Ahead of the Olympics in Los Angeles in 2028, the outlook does not appear to be encouraging.  The obvious message that would be drawn from this overall performance is that the state does not spend enough on developing its sporting talent. After all, China, which won a whopping 341 medals — 169 of them gold — has long had a well funded and formidably organised programme to nurture its sporting talent. That  consistently pays dividends in terms of medal tallies in all major multi-sport events, including the Olympics. In the summer Olympics of 2024, for instance, China came second in the medal tally with 91 gongs.  As an analysis in The Indian Express showed, the Indian programme has not yielded quite the same levels of success. Ahead of this edition of the Asian Games, for instance, the government spent almost ₹98 crore on the Target Olympic Podium Scheme (TOPS). This scheme, started in 2014, focuses on elite athletes and offers intensive customised training and systematic exposure to competition. But the analysis found that only roughly two per cent of the TOPS spending translated into gold medals. Indeed, the recurve gold was not an outcome of the scheme’s interventions.  The ₹98 crore spending is considerably higher than the ₹24.21 crore spent in 2023. The question, then, is not whether India lacks sporting talent but whether the TOPS scheme is identifying the right talent to develop. This is, admittedly, not an easy task and often a question of sheer luck.  That said, there is some long-term hope to be drawn from the stories of Indian sportspersons who have overcome adverse economic conditions to compete in the international arena. R Vithya Ramraj’s is a heart-warming story of a truck driver’s daughter who won multiple medals, including the women’s relay gold. Boxing gold medalist and Olympic bronze medalist Lovlina Borgohain, who came from a family of poor agriculturalists, is another example. Their ability to develop has much to do with significant improvements in access to sporting and training infrastructure compared with the past. The Khelo India Centres that have opened across the country are a case in point. But these are still exceptions rather than standard practice. As the Nagoya reality check shows, India needs to enable more of its people, especially among the poorest, to access sporting facilities. Only then can it discover the critical mass of talent that can win medals at the highest level, consistently.   Topics : Asian Games sports athletes Hockey Business Standard Editorial Comment Editorial Comment

entry.title: Enabling competition
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / Enabling competitionEnabling competition

India must encourage entry of firms and innovation

premium

Representative image for manufacturing

Business Standard Editorial Comment3 min read Last Updated : Oct 05 2026 | 11:06 PM ISTThe latest Monthly Economic Review (MER) from the Ministry of Finance makes an important distinction about what India needs next. It notes that even though the economy remains buoyant, investors are cautious because trade tensions, tariff pressures, geopolitical risks and higher global interest rates are affecting the outlook. India, therefore, cannot take its recent growth performance for granted. Only the right policy environment can encourage investment. In this regard, the MER notes that India must become “more competition-friendly rather than business-friendly”. Only a competitive economy, it argues, can become successful and innovative. Attracting investment and making it easier for businesses to operate are necessary, but they are not sufficient. A business-friendly regime can lower costs and speed up approvals. A competition-friendly economy goes further. It ensures that firms face competitive pressure to improve productivity and quality. For instance, a 2010 International Monetary Fund (IMF) study, using firm-level data across countries, found that competition-enhancing product-market reforms accounted for 12-15 per cent of productivity growth in countries. Meanwhile, a more recent IMF assessment of India argues that weak business dynamism and subdued competition are holding back productivity. It notes that subdued dynamism tends to affect the reallocation of resources towards more productive firms.  Manufacturing is a good test. The MER, for instance, notes that electronics production more than doubled in five years to 2025-26 and exports rose about fivefold, with smartphones becoming India’s largest exported product category. However, most components are still imported and the domestic supplier ecosystem remains incomplete. The next challenge, therefore, is not merely to attract more factories but to deepen backward integration, supplier networks, and increase domestic value addition. Indian products need to be more competitive in global markets. However, competition in the economy cannot be left only to the Competition Commission of India’s (CCI’s) enforcement after a market has already become concentrated or a firm has abused its position. Government policies themselves shape market structure through licensing, procurement, subsidies, tariffs, localisation requirements, access to infrastructure, and sectoral regulation. A policy intended to support domestic capability can build competitive firms, but if poorly designed, it can also protect incumbents from competitive pressure. India has had a draft National Competition Policy since 2011, but it has never been formally implemented. The Parliamentary Standing Committee on Finance last year reiterated the need to implement such a policy and to improve coordination between the CCI and sectoral regulators. It is well known that it is relatively easy for large businesses to operate in India than it is for small and new entrants, partly because of complex regulations that attach a premium to access and the ability to get things done. This is one of the reasons large conglomerates are expanding into multiple areas, potentially affecting the entry of more dynamic and smaller firms.  This needs to change if India is to achieve higher sustainable growth.  The success of several policies, including production-linked incentives, component schemes and semiconductor programmes, should ultimately be judged by whether the sectors that get support can achieve scale, productivity, technological depth, and export competitiveness without requiring permanent protection. The same principle applies beyond manufacturing to aviation, infrastructure, energy, finance, telecom and digital markets. Thus, being competition-friendly requires better regulation, stronger institutions, policy consistency and state capacity. India now needs to move from business-friendly to market-friendly policymaking.   Topics : competition business Investment Business Standard Editorial Comment Editorial Comment

entry.title: Price for the future
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / Price for the futurePrice for the future

Anthropic's IPO will be a test case

premium

Anthropic plans capital expenditures of $518 billion on cloud and compute infrastructure | Image: Bloomberg

Business Standard Editorial Comment Mumbai 3 min read Last Updated : Oct 04 2026 | 10:04 PM ISTThe reported details of Anthropic’s initial public offering (IPO) highlight the stratospheric valuations investors are assigning to artificial intelligence (AI). The IPO documents also flag concern about AI’s tendency to go rogue. Anthropic, which declared $42 billion in 2025 losses, is hoping to raise funds at a valuation of $2 trillion. It is said to have devoted 80 pages of offer documents to grim warnings about the existential threat posed by AI. The prospectus warns that AI models could exhibit “self-preserving behaviours”, including attempts to “resist shutdown”, to “conceal or manipulate information” and behaviour “resembling blackmail”. The company also says that the potential for a model to be aware it was being tested created “significant limitations” for Anthropic’s ability to assess model safety.  There are many examples of dangerous autonomous behaviour by AI. For example, OpenAI’s agents have hacked dozens of websites including AI startup Hugging Face and Australia’s health care system. OpenAI is delaying the release of its latest GPT iteration due to safety concerns. As AI models become smarter, concerns will only grow. Many domain experts assess AI as more dangerous than nuclear weapons due to its ability to become autonomous. The United States (US) administration is taking note of the dangers of what US President Donald Trump now calls “superintelligence”, and suggesting the development of safety standards. But what those standards could be and how long it will take AI to “jailbreak” them are big question marks. AI’s astonishing capabilities are also what lead to astonishing valuations. Anthropic plans capital expenditures of $518 billion on cloud and compute infrastructure. Sector analysts say AI-related investment will absorb over $10 trillion in capex in the next five years. That’s more than twice India’s gross domestic product. Only financiers with very deep pockets can provide this amount and, presumably, they will be seeking big returns on capital. That is an indication of how capable AI is expected to become.  If Anthropic does hit $2 trillion, this would make it the seventh-most valuable listed company. It would overtake SpaceX (market cap of $1.95 trillion) and the SpaceX IPO is worth discussing in this context because it had both AI and Anthropic connections. In May, SpaceX, which has $37 billion in accumulated losses, listed at a valuation of over $1.8 trillion. That was in part because SpaceX is the holding company for xAI, the subsidiary under which Elon Musk holds group AI assets. Anthropic pays SpaceX $1.25 billion a month to rent compute resources. Anthropic’s financials (as reported) are fascinating. It had $4.6 billion in 2025 revenues. That was 12 times what it had made in 2024. It has already logged over $16 billion in revenue in the first two quarters of 2026. In 2025, Anthropic spent $12.6 billion on operations, with $8 billion in operating losses. Another $34 billion was written off. However, the growth is impressive. So are the demonstrable advances made by AI in the past three years. The fears of the damage it can do are realistic. Whether the valuations can be justified, or they are a gigantic bubble, is however, an open question.   Topics : Artificial intelligence IPOs Investment Editorial Comment Business Standard Editorial Comment

entry.title: Policy response
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / Policy responsePolicy response

Compelling reasons for an increase in the repo rate

premium

A discussion paper issued by the RBI last year showed that the inflation rate had declined considerably since the adoption of the flexible inflation-targeting framework (Photo: Reuters)

Business Standard Editorial Comment Mumbai 3 min read Last Updated : Oct 04 2026 | 9:58 PM ISTThe outcome of this week’s meeting of the six-member Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) of the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) will be closely followed. Aside from the decision on the policy rate, the meeting will also mark the completion of 10 years of the MPC. The first MPC meeting was held on October 3 and 4, 2016. A poll conducted by this newspaper last week showed that most economists expected the rate-setting panel to increase the policy repo rate by 25 basis points. There are compelling reasons for the central bank to adjust the policy rate. The consumer price index-based inflation rate increased to 4.8 per cent in August, as against 4.5 per cent in the previous month, and is expected to increase further.  The MPC’s own projections from the last meeting show that the rate is expected to increase to 5.9 per cent in the third quarter this financial year, and would remain above 5 per cent at least until the first quarter next financial year.  It is possible that the inflation projection will be revised upwards. Renewed tensions in West Asia have again pushed up prices of crude oil. It is worth noting that pump prices in India have not been adjusted to fully reflect the higher global prices. Oil-marketing companies are running large under-recoveries, which may not be sustainable if oil prices remain at higher levels in the coming months. Besides, the monsoon has ended with a deficit of about 13 per cent. Although India has large foodgrain stocks, any impact on production, including on the output of perishables, could influence inflation outcomes. The food-inflation rate in August was close to 6 per cent. Furthermore, an inflation rate well above 5 per cent could push the real policy rate close to zero or even into negative territory, which is neither the objective of the monetary policy nor desirable in the present circumstances. Growth is not a concern for the MPC at this point. The Indian economy is growing at a strong pace and expanded by 7.8 per cent in the first quarter this financial year.   Interestingly, the fact that most market participants expect the MPC to increase the repo rate, in a way, reflects how the flexible inflation-targeting framework, adopted a decade ago, has helped evolve market expectations. Since the inflation rate is expected to go well above the target of 4 per cent, the markets expect the MPC to act. Leaving the policy rate unchanged at this stage will require a great deal of explaining and could lead to an adverse market reaction. The framework and functioning of the MPC have substantially increased transparency in the conduct of monetary policy. The RBI has a clear target and objective, with the committee responsible for attaining that objective. The minutes of the meeting are released with the views of each member of the committee. In case the MPC is unable to achieve the objective, as defined in the law, it has to write to the government, explaining the reasons for failure and what it proposes to do to achieve the objective.  A transparent policy framework and action in accordance with it help anchor inflation expectations, which is said to have considerable influence on actual inflation outcomes. A discussion paper issued by the RBI last year showed that the inflation rate had declined considerably since the adoption of the flexible inflation-targeting framework. With expectations getting firmly anchored, this will help the central bank maintain price stability over the medium to long term.   Topics : Inflation Reserve Bank of India repo rate monetary policy Business Standard Editorial Comment Editorial Comment

entry.title: Best of Opinion: Feedback ignored may return as friction, mistrust, failure
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Specials / Best of Opinion: Feedback ignored may return as friction, mistrust, failureBest of Opinion: Feedback ignored may return as friction, mistrust, failure

Healthy systems do not just impose, regulate or command. They also listen, learn and adjust before feedback becomes breakdown

Reetesh Anand New Delhi 3 min read Last Updated : Oct 12 2026 | 6:15 AM ISTStrong systems do not just act but also listen. Tax authorities need to hear what compliance feels like for businesses. Election bodies need to respond to questions about credibility. Electricity markets need to absorb the signal sent by falling renewable costs. Infrastructure planning needs to respect what mountains and rivers are telling us. Democracies, too, weaken when competing sides stop hearing each other. The common lesson across all these issues is that feedback ignored eventually returns as friction, mistrust or failure. Our first editorial today, “From enforcement to trust”, looks at the GST regime after years of aggressive action against evasion and fraud. Enforcement was necessary, but the next stage cannot be built on permanent suspicion. Businesses need simpler procedures, predictable rules, fewer intrusive interventions and a system where compliant taxpayers are not treated as potential offenders by default. The editorial argues for a shift from enforcement-heavy administration towards trust-based compliance. Tax reform matures when the state learns from how the system actually works for those inside it.  The second editorial, “A democratic debate”, turns to the Election Commission of India. Questions about electoral processes should not automatically be treated as attacks on the institution. Credibility is strengthened when concerns are answered, data is disclosed and scrutiny is taken seriously. Democratic institutions do not protect themselves by closing off debate; they strengthen themselves by engaging with it. Ajay Shah’s column, “Consequences of cheap electricity”, looks at the signal sent by falling renewable-energy costs. If clean electricity becomes substantially cheaper, it can reshape industrial location, production costs and competitiveness. But India will benefit only if power markets, transmission, regulation and pricing allow firms to respond to that signal. Cheap power is not just an energy story. It could alter the economic geography of manufacturing, but only if the institutional machinery is flexible enough to let prices guide investment. Sunita Narain’s column, “Himalayan blunders and beyond”, deals with a more physical form of feedback. Repeated landslides, floods and ecological damage in the Himalayas are warnings about the consequences of construction that ignores hydrology, geology and carrying capacity. The problem is not that the mountains have failed to warn us. It is that development repeatedly proceeds as though those warnings could be negotiated away. Better planning requires treating ecological signals as hard constraints, not inconveniences. “When culture wars killed democracy”, Hugh Eakin’s review of Victor Sebestyen’s Weimar Germany, looks back at history. The Weimar Germany experience shows how democratic systems could unravel when political disagreement turns into cultural warfare and rival camps stop recognising each other as legitimate participants. Healthy systems do not just impose, regulate or command. They also listen, learn and adjust before feedback becomes breakdown.

entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Specials / Best of Opinion: Elon Musk should never get a satellite licence in IndiaBest of Opinion: Elon Musk should never get a satellite licence in India

From Starlink's security concerns and Maharashtra's drought politics to challenges facing Modi's third term and Shashi Tharoor's political branding, today's opinions examine a variety of issues

Elon Musk | Image: Bloomberg

Tanmaya Nanda New Delhi 3 min read Last Updated : Oct 10 2026 | 6:15 AM ISTHello and welcome to Best of Business Standard Opinion, our wrap of the day's editorial page.  Examples of oligarchs crying foul cannot be more ironic than Elon Musk accusing Indian tycoons of blocking Starlink. The resistance, however, stems primarily from the government’s security concerns, not Mukesh Ambani or Sunil Mittal, argues R Jagannathan. Satellite communications could help insurgents evade internet shutdowns, while Musk’s political activism and influence abroad raise concerns about foreign interference. The commercial market will initially be limited, with government agencies, businesses and wealthy users likelier customers than poor rural communities. With domestic alternatives being developed, Jagannathan argues that India must retain sovereign control over critical communications infrastructure and deny Musk a satellite licence.  Maharashtra’s deficient monsoon threatens the rabi crop, raising fears of a drought potentially worse than that of 1972. That earlier crisis prompted employment guarantees, food distribution reforms and measures to protect landless labourers. The 2026 Drought Management Code, however, appears inconsistently implemented, with some relatively well-watered areas qualifying for relief while others facing severe shortages are excluded. The resulting scramble for drought relief has become a contest over political patronage and constituency interests, observes Aditi Phadnis. The crisis is temporarily uniting ruling allies and postponing tensions over Chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis, Eknath Shinde and the Shiv Sena’s future. Narendra Modi’s third term faces an unprecedented convergence of political, institutional and economic challenges as he enters his 26th year in public life. The government’s once-dominant narrative of nationalism, welfare delivery and infrastructure development now competes with growing public discontent, notes Shekhar Gupta. He identifies 12 warning signs, including doubts over electoral integrity, judicial credibility, economic performance, government indecision, youth disaffection and shrinking strategic space under Donald Trump. The deeper crisis, he contends, concerns trust in the Constitution, the Supreme Court’s fairness and the Election Commission’s independence. Failure to address these institutional weaknesses could make the run-up to 2029 difficult. Shashi Tharoor has turned his formidable English vocabulary, wit and erudition into a distinctive mass-market political brand, says Sandeep Goyal. After losing the race to become UN Secretary-General, Tharoor entered Indian politics, where his polished English initially attracted controversy but eventually became his signature asset. His 2017 use of “farrago” went viral, spawning memes and a Word of the Day following. Goyal sees this as a lesson in brand differentiation: standing apart can generate visibility more effectively than imitating rivals. Yet Tharoor’s linguistic flair also risks caricature, forcing him to demonstrate that his appeal extends beyond vocabulary to broader political substance and relevance.

entry.title: The making of brand Shashi Tharoor
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / The making of brand Shashi TharoorThe making of brand Shashi Tharoor

The story of the man who makes you open a dictionary before breakfast is a masterclass in accidental differentiation

premium

Mr Tharoor’s brand lesson is simple: In a cluttered market, don’t try to be louder in the same language. Try to be different in a language only you can own (Photo:PTI)

Sandeep Goyal5 min read Last Updated : Oct 09 2026 | 11:40 PM ISTIn India, there are two types of politicians. Type A: Those who rabble-rouse and make you clap or cry. Type B: Those who make you scratch your head and think. In a fun kind of way.   Shashi Tharoor single-handedly created Type B. And then made Type B more famous than Type A.  Ten years ago, he was a second-rung Congress MP from Thiruvananthapuram, known in Lutyens’ circles as “that UN guy who almost became Secretary General”. Respected, erudite, but not exactly someone your driver would discuss. Today, your driver knows him. Your cook knows him. Your 16-year-old knows him because he had to Google “sesquipedalian” after Mr Tharoor posted it on social media.  How did a diplomat with Oxford English become a mass brand in a country that loves three-word slogans? That’s Brand Tharoor. And it’s a masterclass in accidental differentiation. Mr Tharoor’s brand started in failure.  In 2006, he was India’s candidate for United Nations Secretary General. Shashi Tharoor vs Ban Ki-moon. He lost. Mr Tharoor should have won — suave, brilliant, author of five books, perfect UN English. But he didn’t. Most others would have retired to write columns.   Mr Tharoor did the opposite. He came back to India and joined politics — the one profession in India where good English is usually a disqualification.  In 2009, the Congress gave him Thiruvananthapuram. He won. Became minister of state for external affairs. Then came the first tweet that almost ended him. “Will travel in cattle class in solidarity with holy cows.” Talking about economy class. India erupted. In 2009, Twitter (now X) had 200,000 users in India. All of them were outraged. The headlines screamed: “Tharoor insults economy class passengers, calls them cattle.” He apologised.   But the brand was born — the English-speaking, slightly elitist, very witty man. Brand Tharoor pivoted from politician to phenomenon.  The real launch of Brand Tharoor was not a speech. It was a word. In July 2017, he tweeted: “Exasperating farrago of distortions, misrepresentations and outright lies.” India stopped. News anchors who had never used the word “farrago” in 20 years had to say it 20 times that evening. Memes exploded. School kids asked teachers — “What is farrago?”  And then Mr Tharoor did the smartest thing a brand can do — he owned it. He didn’t say: “Sorry for big words.” He launched “Tharoor’s Word of the Day.”  Farrago. Rodomontade. Sesquipedalian. Floccinaucinihilipilification — 29 letters, meaning the “act of estimating something as worthless”. He used it to describe something as worthless, using a word worthless to estimate worthlessness. Suddenly, every Indian who wanted to sound smart had a new guru. English teachers loved him. Tinder bios started saying: “Looking for someone who understands Tharoor without dictionary.”  This is classic brand differentiation. In a market where every politician was trying to be more desi, more simple, Mr Tharoor went the opposite way —  more complex, more English, more Oxford.  Byron Sharp would call it Distinctive Asset. In a sea of white kurta, Hindi slogan sameness, one man in a well-cut suit saying “snollygoster” stands out. You may not like him, but you cannot ignore him.  His English didn’t make him elite. It made him meme-able. In India today, meme-able is electable — at least for mindshare. From 2017 to 2020, Mr Tharoor became India’s most followed politician after Narendra Modi and Rahul Gandhi, without being Prime Minister, without being chief minister, without a single Hindi slogan. That’s not politics. That’s branding.  He turned vocabulary into virality.  The big words have both built and boxed him. For his fans, the words are proof of erudition. For his critics, the words are proof of elitism.  Mr Tharoor’s brand lesson is simple: In a cluttered market, don’t try to be louder in the same language. Try to be different in a language only you can own.  He didn’t try to out-Modi Modi in Hindi oratory. He didn’t try to out-Rahul Rahul in yatra. He owned English, books, wit — assets no one else could copy.  Second lesson: One distinctive word can be bigger than 100 speeches. Farrago did more for Mr Tharoor than 10 years of parliamentary questions.  Third lesson: Every strength, if overused, becomes your caricature. Mr Tharoor’s English got him famous, but now he has to work twice as hard to remind people he is more than English.  Brand Tharoor is not perfect. But it is lovable. In a country of 1.4 billion where most politicians sound the same, a man who makes you open a dictionary before breakfast has already won.  After all, as Mr Tharoor himself would say — his career is not an exasperating farrago, but a compelling case of rodomontade turned into relevance.  And you just Googled rodomontade, didn’t you?  That's Brand Tharoor.  
The writer is chairman of Rediffusion     Disclaimer: These are personal views of the writer. They do not necessarily reflect the opinion of www.business-standard.com or the Business Standard newspaperTopics : Shashi Tharoor Social Media indian politics BS Opinion

entry.title: When the crops wilt
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / When the crops wiltWhen the crops wilt

The drought is almost providential for the ruling party as it postpones the hour of reckoning

premium

Seventy-five per cent of the state is officially stricken by drought and 82 per cent of agriculture is rain-fed with just 18 per cent irrigated area

Aditi Phadnis5 min read Last Updated : Oct 09 2026 | 11:22 PM ISTIf it doesn’t rain in a few weeks, the rabi (winter-spring) agricultural season will also fail, and Maharashtra could be on the edge of a catastrophe after more than an 18 per cent deficiency in rain during the kharif (monsoon) season. Seventy-five per cent of the state is officially stricken by drought and 82 per cent of agriculture is rain-fed with just 18 per cent irrigated area.  Chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis said last month: “We are bracing for severe drought, which could be worse than in 1972.” Revenue Minister Chandrashekhar Bawankule warned workers in Nagpur last month that “as the drought progresses, a bigger crisis will come upon Maharashtra. In fact, it will be bigger than the pandemic. There will be a shortage of water and fodder. You will see kharif and rabi wrecked. All crops will take a hit”. National Congress Party (SP) chief Sharad Pawar repeated the apprehension: “This year’s drought could be worse than in 1972.”  What happens to politics in a drought? Typically, it works out best for the ruling party. Take Mr Pawar. In terms of career progression, 1972 was not at all bad for him. He became a member of the Legislative Assembly (MLA) for the first time from Baramati, and at 32, a state minister in charge of home and general administration in the Vasantrao Naik government. He was sent to other states to secure foodgrain for Maharashtra (he got a cold reception, he writes in his autobiography, from Uttar Pradesh because he refused to touch then chief minister Kamalapati Tripathi’s feet) but many other governments helped Maharashtra out. This eventually led to his star rising.  That 1972 drought was key to teaching India how to manage drought and food shortages. Maharashtra launched the Employment Guarantees Scheme (EGS) in 1969, the first state in India to do so. Research by economist Jean Dreze suggests that the poorest of the poor — agricultural landless labour — who were always the worst-hit in famines, found themselves relatively secure as a result of state intervention. The EGS provided this group a steady source of income and when, combined with the state’s robust public distribution system in the state, Maharashtra prevented the devastation that states like Bihar faced. True, the quality of the work and low payment, the quality of consumption, and the sudden injection of cash-fuelled consumption in a struggling rural economy had its own impact. But as economist Elizabeth Oughton observed in her research, some landless agricultural labour families “enjoyed” the drought because of the guarantee of work it represented.  More policy reform followed. Though only a junior minister, Mr Pawar scrapped the ban on the inter-district movement of fodder. Much later, came the construction of check dams (tiny dams built on nallahs) in the Prithviraj Chavan government (2009), cattle camps run by non-government organisations, and eventually the Drought Management Code (DMC) of 2026.  Although the DMC is rigorous in defining drought, its rollout apparently is not so much. Mahabaleshwar is one of the wettest towns in India. Yet it is on the list of talukas hit by drought and, therefore, eligible for drought relief. How could that happen? Although Maharashtra Deputy Chief Minister Eknath Shinde represents an Assembly constituency in Thane, he belongs to the Mahabaleshwar taluka. And if every farmer — for instance — gets drought relief of ₹1 lakh per hectare and other benefits, so will farmers in Mahabaleshwar! By contrast, Kagal (represented by Hasan Mushrif in Kolhapur district), Shirdi (represented by Radhakant Vikhe Patil in Ahmadnagar district) and Dindori (represented by Narhari Zirwal in Nashik), among others, do not figure on the list, although all three are battling a severe shortage of water and crop failure. All three individuals belong to parties that are in the ruling alliance and are furious that their regions will not be eligible for drought relief.  So power, patronage and money fuel politics in drought: And the ruling party controls all of those. Climate-change activists can scream El Nino till they’re blue in the face. But the fact is, no one in Maharashtra is talking about “differences” between Mr Fadnavis and Mr Shinde for the moment. Instead, there is a wild scramble to get your constituency put on the drought-relief list. Crisis forces unity. In 1972, a young Sharad Pawar saw thousands of women led by Mrinal Gore, Ahilya Rangnekar and others take out the Laatni (rolling pin) morchas (processions) on Bombay streets, protesting against skyrocketing prices, beating empty tins with kitchen ladles.  All that is passe now.  In some ways, the drought is providential because it postpones the hour of reckoning in Maharashtra politics. The Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) has no objection in principle to Mr Shinde, a Maratha, becoming chief minister. In fact, it badly needs a Maratha. But it would like him to merge his party, the Shiv Sena, into the BJP. Sena MLAs are against that move. Having won the Assembly elections and the Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation polls pretty much on his own, Mr Fadnavis knows he is secure. But his followers and supporters are nudging him towards higher ambitions. A good drought is all things to all people!   Disclaimer: These are personal views of the writer. entry.title: The world is not the map
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / The world is not the mapThe world is not the map

A UN-backed push for more accurate world maps highlights how every map involves compromises-and how the way we depict the Earth can shape our view of the world

premium

Africa is about 14 times larger than Greenland, a difference obscured by the commonly used Mercator map projection(Image: Wikimedia Commons)

Atanu Biswas5 min read Last Updated : Oct 09 2026 | 10:27 PM ISTWhile the Earth might be round, the map hanging on my wall is most definitely not. This seemingly innocent observation now has a fresh lease of political life. The United Nations General Assembly endorsed on September 4 an African-led resolution endorsing world maps depicting continents’ sizes proportionally more accurately. It, however, doesn’t ban Mercator projections nor mandate any other form of maps. It merely promotes the greater use of equal area maps, such as Equal Earth maps, especially when it comes to size representation.  The map that we grew up looking at doesn’t only show us locations of countries on Earth but also shapes our view of the world itself. But, let’s take an orange, peel it off delicately, and attempt to flatten all the peel out onto a tabletop. It wrinkles, rips, overlaps, or stretches. This simple experiment illustrates the problem of map-making from its beginning. The Earth is a curve, whereas paper is flat. One can cut and reassemble the peel, but cannot flatten it out completely without some modification. This phenomenon can be described in a reversed way, too: Try to cover an orange by a flat sheet of paper without distortion. Failure to do it doesn’t depend on the paper, but on geometry.  Nearly 200 years ago, in 1827, the legendary German mathematician Carl Friedrich Gauss offered a mathematical explanation to this problem by his Theorema Egregium. The curvature of the sphere is positive, and that of the plane is zero. Their geometrical natures are clearly different. Hence, while we project Earth, we have to give up something. We can keep form, area, some distance, or directions on our map. But we cannot keep all of them. There’s no ideal world map — that’s not a defect of cartography, but the effect of mathematics.  The map most of us use was invented by Gerardus Mercator in 1569. This map was extremely successful because of its practical uses — it was used for navigation as it preserved angles. In terms of its goal, it was an amazing creation. But Mercator has its noticeable drawback — sizes of objects become more and more exaggerated towards the poles. Take Greenland, which seems nearly the same size as Africa. It isn’t. Africa is actually 14 times larger. However, oddly enough, a projection intended for seafarers became the default map of the world in textbooks and also in practice.  An equal-area projection alters this perspective. Though, it doesn’t solve the problem from a mathematical standpoint. It just makes another kind of compromise. The Gall-Peters map preserves area but changes shape. Winkel Tripel tries to reduce multiple distortions. Though Goode Homolosine map projection maintains the proportion of sizes, the oceans have been split into pieces on the map. Equal Earth Projection was created by Tom Patterson, Bojan Savrič, and Bernhard Jenny in 2018. It retains relative size and maintains continent shape.  Which map, therefore, is the right one? Well, correct for what? A sailor would use one map, while a geographer would require another. A geography textbook will have yet another preference. Each map is an expression of the decision made on what to preserve and what to sacrifice.  However, each map is made with certain decisions in mind. Why is north at the top? Why is Europe in the middle? Why is the Pacific always shown on the margins? Nature doesn’t demand that “north” always be placed “up.” An upside-down map makes Australia appear at the top. Centre the Pacific, and the division between East and West starts looking like something completely different. The Earth remains the same. All that has changed is the frame around the picture. A map might begin geometrically, but it can become political.  Certainly one of the finest instances where humanity plays with the world is demonstrated in the movie The Great Dictator (1940) in which Charlie Chaplin played the Hitler-like character Adenoid Hynkel. In the film, Hynkel takes a globe, blows it up, and starts playing with it, throwing it up in the air. For a moment, the whole world is his toy. Then it bursts. While the sequence is comedic, there’s something strangely fitting about imagining the scene in relation to mapping. A globe keeps the curvature of the Earth; a map takes it away. Once the world is flattened, however, it becomes easier to reshape — shift boundaries, change centres, adjust scales. Maps have their own kind of power.  We shouldn’t, however, throw Mercator’s map in the dustbin of history. It still has its uses — for navigation and otherwise — wherever its attributes come in handy. Neither do we want to think that Equal Earth provides the solution. No map does so. Perhaps the truly honest answer is to appreciate the compromises in any map. This, perhaps, is the real message of the UN’s map debate. The earth will continue on just where it was before — round, huge, and completely unconcerned with the squabbles of the map-makers.

From integrated transport planning and uncertainty over Rodtep to the RBI's geopolitical challenges, family business governance, today's opinions examine policy and institutional reform

The Reserve Bank of India needs to plan ahead for geopolitical tensions

Tanmaya Nanda New Delhi 3 min read Last Updated : Oct 09 2026 | 6:15 AM ISTHello and welcome to Best of Business Standard Opinion, our wrap of the day's editorial page.  The Union Cabinet’s approval of an Integrated Transport & Logistics Authority is a welcome step towards ending fragmented planning across roads, railways, ports, aviation, waterways, and urban transport. Today’s first editorial notes that ITLA will prepare a long-term National Transport Master Plan, appraise major projects, monitor implementation, and create a unified transport data repository. Integrated planning could improve capital allocation, reduce duplication, and lower logistics costs, but the authority must have sufficient influence over project selection and investment priorities. Duplication with PM Gati Shakti must also be avoided, while data integration requires interoperability and safeguards. ITLA should ultimately be judged by whether planning changes implementation. The government’s three-month extension of Rodtep provides continuity but little certainty for exporters, who finalise orders well in advance. Keeping existing rates and value caps unchanged does not address concerns arising from the scheme’s uncertain future and sharply lower budget allocation. The second editorial notes that Rodtep refunds embedded taxes rather than providing a conventional export subsidy, making predictability essential for competitiveness. Previous policy changes, including rate restrictions and subsequent restoration, have highlighted the costs of volatility. With exports gaining momentum, the editorial urges a longer extension, greater funding, consultation, a defined transition period, and policy stability to support exporters. The Reserve Bank of India's (RBI) delayed rate hike has left it confronting higher oil prices, surplus liquidity, rising US Treasury yields, narrowing India-US bond spreads, and renewed FII outflows. T T Ram Mohan contends that the central bank should have acted earlier, while arguing that conventional monetary policy frameworks are inadequate in a world where geopolitical disruptions are increasingly routine. He proposes creating a Strategic Affairs unit within the RBI that would bring together expertise in international relations, defence, energy, and economics. Such an unit would assess geopolitical developments, construct scenarios for oil prices, inflation, and exchange rates, and assign probabilities to them, enabling better-informed decisions. India’s family-owned businesses face a new governance challenge: control can now be contested from within, rather than threatened by outside acquirers. Amit Tandon uses the Tata Sons dispute to suggest that promoter stakes may no longer guarantee boardroom control. Families could respond by retaining executive authority, favouring accommodating directors, strengthening governance charters, and simplifying ownership structures. Yet evidence on family control and performance is mixed, with studies showing that professional managers can outperform family CEOs, while family ownership can support stronger returns. The column concludes that succession planning, governance, professional management, and trust between owners and boards will become crucial. Sebastian Mallaby’s The Infinity Machine offers an extensively researched account of Demis Hassabis, DeepMind, and the quest for superintelligence. In his review of the book,Devangshu Datta traces Hassabis’ extraordinary journey from chess and gaming prodigy to neuroscientist and AI pioneer, highlighting DeepMind’s development of AlphaGo, AlphaZero, and AlphaFold, whose protein-folding breakthrough has accelerated drug research. Mallaby, drawing on hundreds of hours of access to Hassabis and his associates, also chronicles DeepMind’s financial struggles, Google’s acquisition, and Silicon Valley’s corporate rivalries and ethical disputes. Datta praises the book’s meticulous sourcing but finds Mallaby less effective at explaining complex technology and insufficiently critical of Hassabis, suggesting that extraordinary access may have compromised objectivity.

entry.title: Seamless connectivity
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / Seamless connectivitySeamless connectivity

Integrated transport planning will bolster mobility

premium

The proposed Integrated Transport & Logistics Authority aims to improve coordination across transport modes and reduce logistics costs

Business Standard Editorial Comment Mumbai 3 min read Last Updated : Oct 08 2026 | 10:44 PM ISTThe Union Cabinet’s approval for the formation of the Integrated Transport & Logistics Authority (ITLA) is a welcome recognition that India’s transport infrastructure cannot be planned effectively in departmental silos. Roads, railways, ports, aviation, inland waterways and urban transport are economically interdependent. Yet investment decisions are still largely taken within individual ministries and agencies, often without adequately considering their implications for the wider transport network. ITLA is intended to address this gap. It will prepare a National Transport Master Plan with a horizon of more than 10 years, assess sectoral and annual plans of transport ministries, technically appraise central infrastructure projects costing ₹500 crore or more, monitor their implementation, and undertake post-project impact assessment. It will also create a National Transport Data Repository, drawing on sources such as goods and services tax eway bills, FASTag, Vahan and other mobility data. The rationale is sound. It is not the objective of the transport policy to maximise investment in individual modes but to minimise the cost and time involved in moving people and goods. A new highway may be valuable, but its economic payoff could depend on the availability of a rail connection, an efficient port, or a logistics hub. Integrated planning can, therefore, improve capital allocation, reduce duplication, and lower logistics costs.  India has often created institutions for coordination without giving them sufficient authority to coordinate. The Unified Metropolitan Transport Authorities (UMTAs), proposed in several cities, have often remained largely advisory because the agencies controlling transport infrastructure, operations and finances continue to function independently. New Delhi’s renewed effort to establish a UMTA is a reminder that even within a single metropolitan area, integration remains difficult when responsibilities and funding are fragmented. The same lesson applies to ITLA. As a special-purpose vehicle under the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade, rather than under a transport ministry, it has the potential to provide a more neutral perspective across modes. But neutrality alone will not make ministries comply with its recommendations. Its appraisal and monitoring functions must have a meaningful bearing on project selection, investment priorities and implementation. Otherwise, the authority risks becoming another layer of consultation. There is also a risk of duplication with PM Gati Shakti.  The proposed data repository could be particularly valuable. India has enormous transport-related data, but it remains dispersed across ministries, operators and platforms. Bringing these together could make it possible to  better understand freight flows, congestion, vehicle utilisation, and passenger demand. But data integration will require common standards, interoperability, and appropriate safeguards, not merely another database. The experience of the National Common Mobility Card (NCMC) offers a useful caution at the urban level. Launched in 2019 with the promise of “One Nation, One Card”, it was meant to allow seamless payments across metros, buses and other transport systems. Yet interoperability has progressed only gradually: As recently as July this year, the government said the NCMC was functional in only 13 metro projects and 11 bus transport corporations. The problem illustrates how difficult genuine integration can be. ITLA should, therefore, be judged not by the quality of its master plan but by whether that plan changes investment and implementation.     Topics : Transport infrastructure logistics roads Business Standard Editorial Comment Editorial Comment

entry.title: Policy stability
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / Policy stabilityPolicy stability

Exporters need greater certainty in tax-remission policy

premium

The external environment is challenging and India needs to push exports both to attain stability in its external account and to grow at higher rates

Business Standard Editorial Comment Mumbai 3 min read Last Updated : Oct 08 2026 | 10:37 PM ISTThe government’s recent decision to extend the Remission of Duties and Taxes on Exported Products (Rodtep) scheme by only three months, to December 31, provides continuity but little certainty. The Directorate General of Foreign Trade has kept the existing rates and value caps unchanged during the extension period. Exporters typically finalise shipment orders well in advance, making it difficult to factor in the tax remission while determining prices when the continuation remains uncertain. Rodtep’s expenditure was ₹18,313 crore in 2024-25, while the 2025-26 revised estimate (RE) stood at ₹18,233 crore. For 2026-27, however, the Budget estimate was cut to ₹10,000 crore, 45 per cent below the previous year’s RE.  Rodtep is not an export incentive or subsidy in the conventional sense. It returns the embedded central, state and local taxes and levies that exporters have paid, such as those which cannot otherwise be refunded, including taxes on fuel, electricity duties and mandi charges. Its purpose is to ensure that taxes are not exported with the goods. The scheme was introduced in 2021 to replace the Merchandise Exports from India Scheme and align India’s export-support framework with World Trade Organization guidelines. The case for greater predictability is strengthened by the scheme’s scale. It covers more than 10,700 export-product categories, covering diverse sectors of the economy, and as of March 31, 2025, disbursements under the scheme had crossed ₹57,976.78 crore since its launch, underscoring its significant role in supporting India’s merchandise exports. India’s exports are also gaining momentum. According to the commerce ministry’s latest trade data, cumulative merchandise exports rose 17.85 per cent to $215.91 billion during April-August 2026-27, from $183.21 billion in the corresponding period a year earlier.  Notably, the scheme has already seen policy volatility. In February, the government restricted Rodtep rates and value caps to 50 per cent of the prevailing levels. The rates were restored at the end of March after disruption in West Asia affected shipping routes, schedules and logistics costs. While the decision was a response to an exceptional external shock, it highlighted the difficulties exporters faced when policy changes after prices had already been negotiated with overseas buyers. Recognising this, the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Commerce has recommended that any future revision of Rodtep rates be preceded by structured consultation with industry stakeholders and accompanied by a clearly defined minimum transition period. This would help ensure that exporters are not forced to absorb losses on orders contracted on the basis of earlier rates. The commerce ministry has itself sought a five-year extension and an increase in the allocation of funds under the scheme. The government should consider the request and provide exporters a stable policy environment. The external environment is challenging and India needs to push exports both to attain stability in its external account and to grow at higher rates. The least the government should aim to do is to keep the domestic policy environment stable and not add to the complexities that exporters are anyway facing.     Topics : Export incentive Exports Indian exports Merchandise exports Business Standard Editorial Comment Editorial Comment

entry.title: Tata rift echoes beyond Bombay House
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Tata rift echoes beyond Bombay HouseTata rift echoes beyond Bombay House

A bigger stake once secured control, but businesses now see the need for a new playbook

premium

Bombay House

Amit Tandon5 min read Last Updated : Oct 08 2026 | 10:26 PM ISTIn 1983, Swraj Paul tried to take control of Escorts and Delhi Cloth and General Mills (DCM) by buying their shares on the market. By various accounts, he acquired 7.5 per cent in Escorts, while the Nanda family controlled around 5 per cent, and 13 per cent of DCM, compared with the Shri Ram family’s 10 per cent. Though Paul eventually withdrew his bid, the episode exposed how  many families controlled large companies with single-digit stakes until then, relying on the support of state-owned financial institutions. Their obvious response to this attack was to raise their ownership. Today, promoter shareholding in the Nifty500 averages around 50 per cent.  More than four decades later, the challenge for controlling-shareholders comes not from outside, but from within. On September 17, the Tata Sons board reappointed N Chandrasekaran and cleared the path to listing the company, over the opposition of Noel Tata, chairman of Tata Trusts, which owns 66 per cent of Tata Sons and seen as the keeper of its values, fears that a listing will dilute its charter.   Business families will read the dispute as a warning that ownership alone does not guarantee control of the boardroom, overturning an article of faith since 1983 — that a bigger stake is the surest defence. The fallout is likely to play out across at least four fronts.  First, more families may choose to keep control as chairperson  or in an executive capacity, rather than hand it to professional managers. A 2024 Deloitte study of 41 Nifty 50 companies (excluding public-sector enterprises) found that 31 were run by non-promoter chief executive officers and only 10 by promoters. Across India Inc as a whole, the share is likely to be lower still, given that about two-thirds of the S&P BSE 500 companies are family-owned. This episode could slow, or even reverse, the move towards professionalising businesses.  Will this impact India Inc’s performance? Families can point to evidence that ownership commitment pays. Credit Suisse’s Family 1000 research found that since 2006, family- or founder-owned listed companies have outperformed non-family companies by an annual average of 370 basis points. And in India, a study of 4,056 promoter-owned listed firms found that in group-affiliated companies, the level of promoter ownership had no effect on performance.  But the evidence cuts both ways. A landmark study of Danish firms found that when the CEO role passed to a family member, operating profitability fell by at least four percentage points. Even Credit Suisse found that family-owned companies score slightly lower on corporate governance than their non-family peers. A study covering 131 large listed Indian companies shows family firms with non-family CEOs performed better than those with family CEOs. Owning a company is different from running it.  Second, promoters may lean towards independent directors who are unlikely to challenge them. India’s problem is not too few independent directors but the wrong ones, appointed through processes that favour reputation over capability. Tuhin Kanta Pandey, chairman of the Securities and Exchange Board of India, has urged boards to recruit independent directors from beyond cosy networks and equip them to dissent, observing that “a board that never disagrees is not aligned — it’s asleep”. If promoters respond by packing boards with pliant directors, they will weaken the very oversight that minority shareholders rely on. And as one promoter told Business Standard, long-serving professionals can build fiefdoms and fill boards with people unlikely to challenge them.  Third, families will revisit their governance charters, since professionalising a board need not mean sidelining promoters. Companies will spell out who sets strategy, who executes it, and how disagreements are resolved, often through Articles of Association listing reserved matters that need promoter approval. Expect tighter affirmative voting rights, explicit rules on how nominee directors must vote, and clauses on replacing nominee directors and breaking board deadlocks, though nominees still owe their fiduciary duty to the company, not to whoever appointed them.  Yet drafting has limits. No document can fully anticipate a split within the owning family. And if affirmative rights written into charter documents do not hold, foreign direct investors, who rely on such rights, may grow more cautious.  Fourth, families will streamline their shareholding. Many groups still carry layers of crossholdings, investment companies and informal arrangements dating back decades. Families will collapse these into single holding vehicles, trusts or even individual names, to put control on a clearer legal footing. This is critical because today’s fault lines often run within families, not with outsiders — the Chhabrias at Finolex, the Kirloskars, the Kalyanis and Hiremaths — to name just a few.  These cases show how fragile even documented settlements, holding companies, trusts and wills can be.  In 1983, families protected control by raising their stakes. A bigger stake may not be enough if pressure comes from within. The current episode exposes friction that legal drafting cannot resolve. The businesses that come through will be those that plan succession early, apply their own rules consistently and leave management to professionals — they can work with. Such relationships rest on mutual trust and a shared long-term vision. The question now will no longer be whether someone is the best CEO in the market, but whether the controlling and minority shareholders, the boards and managements will align, to pull in the same direction.

entry.title: Geopolitical risks and monetary policy
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Geopolitical risks and monetary policyGeopolitical risks and monetary policy

Central banks need to factor in geopolitical risks before they materialise, not treat them as a sideshow

premium

Illustration: Binay Sinha

T T Ram Mohan6 min read Last Updated : Oct 08 2026 | 10:06 PM ISTLast May, the rupee came under pressure, rising above 96 to the dollar. In June, the Reserve Bank of India announced several measures to facilitate concessional swaps for foreign inflows, notably through the foreign currency non-resident (Bank) or FCNR(B) deposits. The expectation then was that these measures would result in inflows of around $50 billion and help ease the pressure on the rupee.  Your columnist had argued at the time that, given the outlook for oil prices and foreign institutional investor (FII) outflows, the inflow of funds under the RBI schemes would not suffice. A rise in the policy rate was inevitable. The inevitable has happened. The Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) opted for a 25 basis points increase in the repo rate on October 7.  The inflows under the RBI’s special measures amounted to a staggering $143 billion. Yet the rupee trades now at around 96.79 to the dollar. After a two-month hiatus, the exodus of FII funds resumed in September with net outflows of $6 billion.  The economic environment has changed materially in two respects since June. The price of crude oil has gone up from $85-90 to over $100 now. This is the price of oil futures. The market price of crude futures does not reflect the landed cost to India. The government’s chief economic advisor says that the price of India’s oil import basket is $114 today. That is an increase of 61 per cent over the average price of $71 in FY26. We now face oil prices well above our comfort range.  The second factor is the decision of the United States Federal Reserve last month to raise the policy rate by 25 basis points. The betting is that more rate hikes by the Fed are in the offing as inflation in the US remains above the target.   Any rise in Treasury yields affects India in two ways. One, it results in an exit of funds from emerging markets in general, which causes the rupee to depreciate. Two, it results in a narrowing of the yields on 10-year bonds in the US and in India. At 195 basis points, the difference in yields on 10-year government bonds is at its lowest in five years. This factor, too, contributes to the downward pressure on the rupee.  The RBI does not wish to defend any particular value of the rupee. Nevertheless, it has to respond to a sharp depreciation in the rupee because that can stoke domestic inflation.  The measures announced in June have not been able to contain the rupee’s depreciation. They ended up creating surplus liquidity in the system, about half of which has since been mopped up by the RBI. Surplus liquidity in the system renders the transmission of rate hikes that much more difficult.  Thus, by deferring a rate hike in June and August, the RBI is now having to deal with several issues: Higher oil prices, surplus liquidity, higher US Treasury yields, a narrower differential between long-term yields in the US and India, and a continued exodus of FII funds. A pre-emptive hike in the policy rate would have made its job easier. It would conceivably have eased the requirement for intervention through dollar sales in the foreign exchange market.  Monetary policy is said to be forward-looking. However, there is a serious limitation to how “forward-looking” is understood today. Central banks (and international agencies) tend to take a view on the economic situation, outline a baseline forecast and say it is subject to “geopolitical risks”.  In a world in which geopolitical risks are pretty much the norm, such an approach will not do. Central banks cannot afford to react to geopolitical risks — wars, sanctions, trade conflicts — after these have materialised. They will need to factor geopolitical risks explicitly into monetary policy, not treat them as a sideshow. How long will conflicts stretch out? What would that mean for energy prices and supply chain disruptions? Central banks need to ask and answer questions such as these in conducting monetary policy.  In June and August, the questions that needed to be asked were: One, does the US-Iran conflict have a reasonable chance of resolution? And, two, if it does not, what does that bode for oil prices? The answers should have been clear enough. The Iranian and American positions on the core issues were (and still are) so far apart that there was little chance of an amicable resolution. And that meant the continued disruption of oil supplies and an inexorable climb in oil prices to well above the $85-90 range. The implications of oil prices rising above $100 and staying there should have been factored into monetary policy.  Central banks need to create a Strategic Affairs unit that includes people with expertise in international relations, defence studies, the energy sector and economics. The idea is not to replicate the work done in ministries and intelligence agencies. Central banks cannot be in the business of forecasting wars. Rather, the unit must liaise with the concerned agencies and obtain and process geopolitical intelligence relevant to maintaining economic stability.  Central banks know how to respond if there is a major disruption that causes oil prices to rise to $120. What they need is a distribution of probabilities about the disruption. The MPC would have before it, say, a baseline forecast of oil prices of $85-90 per barrel with a 30 per cent probability that oil prices would rise to $120 following a major disruption in the Strait of Hormuz. It would then be better placed to judge whether a rate hike and the associated sacrifice of growth are justified.  The distribution of probabilities is precisely what the Strategic Affairs unit would seek to determine. The unit would convert the assessments it receives into scenarios for oil prices, inflation and exchange rates with probabilities attached to each scenario.   The RBI’s biannual Monetary Policy Report provides fan charts for inflation and gross domestic product  growth, indicating a range of outcomes. These are statistical probabilities based on historical modelling. What is required is scenario-building for current geopolitical risks of the sort outlined above.  Creating a Strategic Affairs unit would signal to the world that the appreciation of geopolitical risks has moved centre-stage at the RBI.
